chunks: When not to use decoupling capacitors. The question: When should you not use decoupling capacitors?
A capacitor next to a chip is the right default, but not an absolute rule. Some regulators and amplifiers become unstable if you add more capacitance than the datasheet allows.
A big capacitor can also cause a huge surge of current at power-on. And a capacitor on a signal line is not decoupling at all. It just slows the signal down.
Think of shock absorbers on a car. The right ones smooth a bumpy road. The wrong ones make the car bounce or fight the steering.
The same part that helps in one setup hurts in another. A capacitor is a shock absorber for voltage, so you match it to what it is attached to.
When a live supply is connected, the cable inductance, the capacitor's ESR and its capacitance form a series RLC.
Ceramic capacitors have tiny ESR, so the circuit is lightly damped.
Inrush current: the surge that flows into an empty capacitor when power is first applied.
Stability: whether a regulator or amplifier settles to a steady output instead of ringing or swinging on its own.
ESR window: the range of internal resistance some regulators need in their output capacitor to stay stable.
Capacitive load limit: the most capacitance an amplifier or reference can drive without ringing. Hot-plug: connecting a live supply to a board whose capacitors are empty.
Plug a 12 volts supply into a board with 100 microfarads of capacitance, and let the voltage rise over 1 milliseconds.
The current that fills the capacitor is i equals C dV over dt equals 100 micro F times 12 volts over 1 milliseconds equals 1. 2 amps.
That can trip a protection circuit sized for a small load. If the voltage jumps up instantly, the surge is far bigger, limited only by wiring resistance. That is the whole idea.
"Decoupling is the default, so the exceptions are specific.
Don't add capacitance beyond what the datasheet allows: LDOs with ESR windows, references and op-amp outputs with capacitive-load limits.

Be careful where capacitance causes problems: hot-plugged inputs where ceramic plus cable inductance overshoots toward twice the input, large capacitors that cause inrush, and bad value mixes that create anti-resonance.
And never decouple a signal line, because that is just a low-pass filter."
